items.title: Bill Huntington and Charlie Suhor Interview, 1992-04-06
items.q: Al, you know, pushed through having Richie Payne on his band

ctx.x: It's in the 60s. It's in the 60s. It kind of could end downbeat series very, very clearly.

But, I mean, at the time, you would have some of the very greatest jazz musicians, modernists playing in one of the rooms, you know, and that's where I first met Ellis. There's an interesting story that Ellis has related on a television program recently that he did. And I remember this incident, too. I was playing with a pianist by the name of Eddie Finassi, and Ellis hit a trio with Marshall Smith and James Black, and they were playing upstairs in the room upstairs. And, by the way, Al Boleto was an early…

So, before you get too far into your bass stuff, I wanted to pick up on something you said about your lack of a peer group when you were with Lawrence Marrero and the black musicians. That was one thing that I think is very unique about you, the fact that of all the players like myself and others who came up with Dixieland as our love, we just didn't have that deep connection with the early traditional players. And it's easier conceptually to pick up the fluff aspects of Dixieland. It's very difficult, it sounds…
